title: Why people are burning Waymos
content:

For the past 24 hours on X, tech people, right wing figures and the media have been posting about Waymos being set on fire in downtown Los Angeles. The Waymos were burned during this weekend’s protests against ICE. I saw them burning and documented it on X and spoke to a couple people in the ground about it.

Overall, people in Los Angeles love Waymos. They’re easy and convenient rides in a city with abysmal public transit options and poor, car-centric city planning. Los Angeles Waymos have largely been immune from the type of attacks that have happened in San Francisco, for instance, where the cars have become a symbol of gentrification and battles over public transit funding.

As more people begin to understand how Waymos operate, however, and what the company’s policies are regarding sharing footage and data with the police, I do think we will start to see more Waymo attacks.

In April, 404 Media revealed that the LAPD was publishing crime footage it got from a Waymo driverless car in an effort to identify a suspect. As 404 reported, “The proliferation of Waymo cars also means the proliferation of roving surveillance cameras. LAPD has shown an interest in obtaining footage from autonomous vehicles that operate in the city; last year we reported on a case in which the LAPD obtained footage from an autonomous food delivery robot to investigate a crime.”

As police begin to leverage tech like Waymo cars, protesters are becoming more aware of the surveillance infrastructure being built into modern life. Many activists have called attention to the fact that social platforms, like Meta, have handed user data over to the police. (In 2022, Facebook handed the data of a mother and daughter facing criminal charges for allegedly carrying out an illegal abortion to law enforcement). And more of the public is becoming aware of tools like facial recognition software, that the police have begun to use heavily.

When I asked a few protesters on the ground yesterday why they thought the Waymos were burning, they told me that the cars “spy” on people and could be recording protest footage. We still don’t know who exactly set fire to the cars or why, but it’s clear that more people are perceiving Waymos as an extension of the police surveillance infrastructure.

The All In podcast is having an existential crisis

After launching in 2020, the All‑In Podcast skyrocketed to success and became the tech podcast among Silicon Valley types. The show is hosted by investors Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, David Sacks, and David Friedberg. It initially covered mostly tech and business, but over the past year the show leaned hard into politics and specifically Donald Trump.

The four co-hosts were essentially a cog in the Musk and Trump machine. Sacks helped rally tech support for Trump’s 2024 campaign (even landing a Trump appointed role as White House crypto "czar") and the podcast hosted Trump on the show during the campaign. The men are also incredibly close to Musk and Calacanis follows Musk around like a puppy dog.

Since the Musk/Trump feud blew up last Friday, however, the podcast has gone dark. The hosts seem to be scrambling and, like many right wing influencers, are now trying to figure out what side to take in order not to alienate their audience.

I think this could be the nail in the coffin for the show’s cultural relevance. It was already slipping, and TBPN, aka “technology's daily show” (formerly the Technology Brothers Podcast), is ascendent. Entrepreneurs John Coogan and Jordi Hays are younger, more in touch with broader culture, and have a humor and self awareness about all the Silicon Valley craziness that a bunch of old rich Silicon Valley millionaires could never emulate. Their show is also formatted for Gen Z, with a livestreamed daily show, robust video presence and focus on business and tech rather than political posturing.

The menswear guy finally did a bad take

The Menswear Guy, Derek Guy, became a Twitter celebrity after Elon Musk took over the platform and Musk’s algorithm suddenly began inserting his content into everyone’s feed. Since then he’s become a beloved character in large part because of his ability to eviscerate anyone who challenges him on men’s clothing, especially right wingers. He does takedowns of far right figures’ clothing, and critiques right wing influencers like Andrew Tate and has advocated for progressive political policies.

All of this has led to him becoming a beloved figure in the broader left internet world. However, over the weekend he decided to weigh in on immigration. “I admire the courage of people protesting the ICE raids in California,” he posted. “I'm against violent protests and think they're counterproductive. I also think that non-violent protests send a more powerful and enduring message.”

He added that he has “long believed in Dr. King's message about using non-violent resistance” before suggesting that instead of going out in the streets to protest ICE, “you can volunteer with pro-immigrant organizations, offer material aid, or even pursue a career in immigration law.” He followed up by suggesting that “If you're in a relationship with an undocumented immigrant, you can make a direct impact on their life by marrying them.”

This obviously set of a wave of backlash. Many pointed out that the protests against ICE raids happening in L.A. were peaceful, and that it was the police who had engaged in violent acts by shooting journalists and peaceful protesters. Also, marrying an immigrant doesn’t seem to do much. Just look at the detention of Mahmoud Khalil.

He eventually followed up with a long post about his family’s personal history immigrating from Vietnam. People didn’t care though. For so long the Menswear Guy has been untouchable, and I think there’s been a lot of pent up resentment towards him that finally has an outlet. As I’ve written before, people feel a lot of gratification when an influencer they already didn’t like for some arbitrary reason does or says something objectively dumb or bad because it gives them a moral justification for that hatred. I do think what Menswear Guy said was dumb and lacking context, but it’s also a lesson in putting anyone with over 1 million followers on a political pedestal.
